entries.title: World War II
entries.reason: No subject the corpus can support: 36 claims from exactly two sources, one on Marian prophecy and one on postwar Nazi technology evacuation, and we hold no source about the Second World War. It also asserted, unattributed and in Anomalica's own voice, that Germany annexed the Sudetenland in March 1938 (it was 1-10 October 1938) one sentence before correctly dating the Anschluss to 1938-03-12. A rebuild fixes the false assertion by attributing it; it cannot give the page a subject.
entries.how_to_reverse: git checkout <retirement commit>^ -- <page>; remove the URL's entry from site/data/redirects.yaml; push both; site deploys.

entries.reason: One bug fix, not 112 retirements. The page for the 2004 USS Nimitz encounter had accumulated 234 alias slugs. 112 of them name entirely different events - the 1947 Kenneth Arnold sighting, the 1948 Mantell incident, the 1950 McMinnville photographs, the 1964 Socorro landing - and every one was live and served the Nimitz article, so a reader following a link about Kenneth Arnold arrived at a 2004 carrier encounter. None of the 112 has a correct destination, because those events have no pages, so they now 404: the honest answer, and better than the wrong one they were giving. A further six slugs were REPAIRED rather than removed - see also_repaired - taken off Nimitz and put on the events that own them. The aliases were emitted correctly from what the graph held against that node at the time; the graph has since been corrected and a build-time assertion now refuses an alias naming a live node the page does not cover. No page file was removed; these were never files. Assembler fbce99b added the assertion, content da6ac25 made the change.
entries.decided_by: anomalica/assembler, verified against production by anomalica/site
entries.how_to_reverse: git revert the commit that removed them; the URLs resolve again on the next deploy.

also_repaired.note: Not retired. These six slugs were taken off the Nimitz page and put on the events they actually belong to, so they still resolve - verified 200 and redirecting correctly on production after the deploy.

entries.corrected: 2026-09-08: first recorded as 118 URLs. That was a per-page set difference - aliases lost FROM THE NIMITZ PAGE - and six of them had moved to other pages rather than stopping. A URL only dies when NOTHING serves it, so the scope has to be every page. Corrected to 112 after the site workspace compared against production and both of us recomputed corpus-wide. The wrong number claimed six live, correctly-redirecting URLs were retired, which is the one error a record like this must not carry.

entries.title: France
entries.reason: A bare country, which the extraction prompt explicitly forbids as a node. Its claims are a real subject with nowhere to attach: French official UFO research conducted independently of and sceptically towards American conclusions, with Jacques Vallee carrying European sighting data into Project Blue Book. That subject has no node, so the claims found the nearest available place. This page is evidence of a missing node rather than of surplus content; see Kanban card PVTI_lADOEBXr0s4BbLkKzg59GiE.

entries.title: USA, California, San Diego
entries.reason: Not a page about San Diego. Four of its paragraphs retell the 2004 USS Nimitz encounter, which has its own page and which this page's own text places about 100 kilometres off the coast, midway between San Diego and Ensenada - so the page states that its own subject did not happen there, and gives a worse account of an article that already exists. The remainder is not about the city either: David Fravor's earlier night landing is about Fravor, and Bruce Leininger attending a Natoma Bay reunion is a reincarnation case that shares nothing with this page but a place name. A place earns a page when things happen at it repeatedly; one event 100 kilometres offshore, told four times, plus two strays, is not a cluster.
